gold_with_text_not_included.reason: I1 and I2 not met; E3 met: participants identified externally presented slot machines, with rewards independent of their responses. Reward uncertainty was manipulated, but the high-versus-low uncertainty contrast measured anticipation during a delay rather than risky/ambiguous choice or perceptual decision difficulty. The paper explicitly describes processing independent of any decision. Group-level whole-brain contrasts are reported (I3 met), and the healthy adult sample meets I4.

I2 not met: exploratory > exploitative trials were defined by choosing a lower versus highest expected-value slot. An admitted high- versus low-risk/uncertainty comparison or task-versus-active-control comparison was not demonstrated. Exploration was not established as uncertainty-directed, so lower expected value cannot establish greater risk or ambiguity. Original human gambling fMRI and whole-brain task activations satisfy I1, I3 and I4. E1 does not apply because a direct condition comparison exists; the exclusion concerns its failure to establish an admitted I2 contrast.

E6 met: uncertain > certain action selection was analyzed voxelwise, but the reported activation map and Table 2 contain only stimulant-users > controls differences in that contrast. Personality correlations use those group-difference clusters or a striatal ROI. No accompanying unmasked whole-brain within-group task effect is reported; the discussion explicitly reserves within-group analyses for future work. The fMRI task, uncertainty comparison, and participant groups otherwise qualify (I1–I4 met).

I2 not met: the reported contrasts concern reward magnitude, higher versus lower gain probability, gains versus losses, and expected-value/prediction-error patterns. An admitted riskier-versus-surer or risk-versus-active-control contrast is not demonstrated. I3 not met: an eligible unmasked whole-brain target result is not demonstrated; reporting focuses on frontal/subcortical regions and applies small-volume correction for hypothesized regions. This does not establish that all analyses were ROI-only (E4 unclear). Human fMRI during monetary guessing and the adult samples satisfy I1 and I4. Exclusion is not based on absent coordinate tables or baseline-only comparisons.

I2 not met: the planned comparison is success versus failure (20% versus 80% errors); the explicitly described whole-brain main effects favor 20% over 80% errors. High-error increases are discussed in regions identified by group-by-error interactions. An admitted higher-risk/uncertainty > lower-risk/uncertainty or task > active-control whole-brain contrast is not demonstrated. I1, I3 and I4 are met: human fMRI during uncertain two-choice prediction, whole-brain error-rate results, and eligible participants. The main error-rate effect in Table 3 means E6 does not apply.

High-risk > low-risk comparisons are reported (I2 met), but their inference uses cingulate small-volume correction. Whole-brain findings concern risk-aversion correlations and an interaction; an eligible unmasked whole-brain condition main effect is not demonstrated (I3 not met). Participants performed scanned risky choices (I1, I4 met). E4 does not apply because other whole-brain analyses are reported.

Human fMRI during perceptual categorization and the degraded > intact visual comparison satisfy I1/I2; the adult sample satisfies I4. I3 is not met: the condition-contrast results in Tables 1 and 2 are restricted to a 11,334-voxel stimulus > fixation functional mask, with correction within that volume. An unrestricted whole-brain result for the eligible hard > easy contrast is not demonstrated. The separately described whole-brain response-time association is not an admitted condition contrast. E4/E5/E6 do not apply: the study also reports voxelwise activation analyses and within-group main effects, alongside DCM.

E6 met: all reported activation maps and Table 2 coordinates compare abstinent versus satiated task effects, constituting session-by-task interactions. The authors explicitly state that general task activation was not reported; no accompanying unmasked within-session task effect is provided. Risky decision making versus an active color-response control was modeled (I2), and group whole-brain voxelwise activation was analyzed (I3). The adult smoker sample qualifies under I4; exclusion concerns the reported contrasts.

I1 and I2 met: participants performed the Iowa Gambling Task during fMRI with an active non-gambling control task. However, individual and group analyses were restricted to anatomical VMPFC masks; no whole-brain task map was reported (I3 not_met; E4 met).

I3 was not demonstrated for the qualifying activation contrast. Fourteen adults performed perceptual categorization during fMRI (I1/I4 met), and the text describes greater univariate RCZ activation for low versus high visibility (I2 met). However, the explicitly documented group-level whole-brain maps are searchlight decoding-accuracy maps. The supplied text does not establish that the supplementary univariate visibility contrast was a group-level whole-brain activation analysis; its supplementary methods and Table 2 are not present in the supplied inputs. Whole-brain decoding alone does not establish I3 for the activation contrast.

I2 not met: an admitted condition-versus-condition or task-versus-active-control contrast was not demonstrated. Decision-phase results primarily concern parametric correlations with explosion probability. The reported planned decision contrast is ChooseWin*P(explode) minus ChooseInflate*P(explode), a safe-minus-risky modulation comparison, rather than an admitted risky-greater-than-safe or high-risk-greater-than-low-risk condition contrast. Human BART fMRI, group whole-brain analyses, and participant eligibility satisfy I1, I3, and I4. E1 does not apply because a comparison between decision regressors is reported, although its form fails I2.

I2 not met: an admitted low-coherence > high-coherence, hard > easy, or perceptual-task > active-control contrast is not demonstrated. Table 1 reports positive/negative parametric coherence effects across four levels; searchlight results classify motion or choice direction against chance. The motion localizer defines individual MT+/V5 ROIs, not a qualifying group decision-task contrast. I1, I3 and I4 met: adults performed perceptual motion decisions during fMRI, and group voxelwise task-evoked univariate maps are reported.

I1, I2 and I4 are met: adults performed the IGT during fMRI, with a defined bad-deck > good-deck risk contrast. I3 is not met: a qualifying group-level whole-brain task-activation effect is not demonstrated. Reported whole-brain findings are correlations of risk contrasts with decision quality/message effectiveness and between-group ANCOVAs; described main-effect comparisons are between groups within selected ROIs. Supplementary main effects are referenced, but their contrasts and whole-brain within-group status are not established in the supplied text or table. Whole-brain correlation analyses prevent classifying this as ROI-only or exclusively between-group. The 25 non-SD participants were reused from Krawitz et al. (2010); overlap itself is not an exclusion criterion.

I2 not met: no admitted risk-versus-safety, high-versus-low-risk, or risky-task-versus-active-control contrast is demonstrated. Table 1 reports pump-number parametric effects separately for pumping and cashing out; Table 2 compares these slopes after explosions versus cash-outs, a prior-outcome comparison rather than an admitted risk contrast. Although white-balloon control trials were included, no active-versus-control activation result is reported. I1, I3 and I4 are met by BART fMRI in 60 adults with group-level whole-brain maps. E2 does not apply to these fMRI maps; PET separately measured receptor availability in a subset.

E6 met: the reported whole-brain results are relapse-group-by-decision interactions, without an accompanying unmasked whole-brain within-group risky > safe task effect. Risky versus safe activation differences within groups are described in insular clusters selected by the interaction. The study otherwise uses original task fMRI during the Risky Gains Task in eligible adults with methamphetamine dependence (I1, I2, I4 met). Whole-brain interaction results are explicitly reported in supplementary materials (I3 met; E4 not met).

The Cups Task compares risky and certain choices during fMRI in qualifying youth samples (I1, I2, I4 met). Table 2/Figure 2 report an omnibus group-by-condition-by-choice ANOVA. Within-group risky/nonrisky effects are subsequent decompositions of the identified regions, while Table 3A/B report anxiety correlations. An accompanying unmasked, whole-brain within-group risky-versus-nonrisky task map was not demonstrated (I3 not_met; E6 met).

I1 and I4 met: healthy adults performed risky-versus-certain gambling during fMRI. Group-level whole-brain searchlight statistical maps include post-choice activity (I3 met). However, these test MVPA pattern discriminability, using within-condition versus between-condition correlations and d > 0, rather than an admitted directional risky > safe or risk > certainty activation contrast (I2 not met). A qualifying gambling > active-control activation contrast is also not demonstrated; the counting distractor was not used in such a comparison.

E6 met: risky-gains fMRI includes risky-versus-safe comparisons and whole-brain group statistics, but reported condition effects are group/subgroup differences or interactions (Tables 3–6). Table 4 describes within-group signal differences only in interaction-selected clusters, not an independent unmasked whole-brain task contrast. Within-group analyses of substance exposure and behavior (including Table 7) are covariate regressions rather than mean condition effects. An accompanying unmasked whole-brain within-group risky-versus-safe task effect is not demonstrated. The participant groups are eligible.

I2 not met: the reported decision-phase effects are linear and quadratic parametric modulations by gain-loss ratio, with additional loss-aversion and gambling-severity associations. No admitted risky-versus-safe, high-versus-low-risk, or risk-task-versus-active-control contrast is demonstrated. Empty pie-chart baseline trials do not provide an active control task. Human gambling fMRI and eligible participants satisfy I1/I4. Group-level whole-brain within-group activation results are present (I3 met; E4/E6 not met), but do not supply the required condition comparison.

I2 not_met: the whole-brain task result tests continuous risk modulation by probability of balloon explosion (Pumpsparametric), without a demonstrated condition-versus-condition or task-versus-active-control contrast of an admitted form. I1, I3 and I4 are met: 21 adult smokers performed BART during fMRI, with group one-sample whole-brain activation and coordinates in Table 1. Despite the resting-state focus, this is not a connectivity-only, ROI-only or between-group-only study (E4, E5 and E6 not_met).

I2 not met: the complete text and original coordinate tables report parametric effects of risk, expected value and belief updating, plus correlations and connectivity, without demonstrating an admitted decision-condition or task-versus-active-control contrast. The accept/reject regressor was a nuisance covariate, not a reported target contrast. I1, I3 and I4 met: 24 adults made risky choices during fMRI, and group whole-brain task activation maps were reported.

I2 not met: the reported whole-brain analyses compare follow-up with baseline risk/reward parametric slopes and correlate those longitudinal changes with substance use. The full text and Table 4 do not demonstrate an admitted risky-versus-safe, high-versus-low risk, or risk-versus-active-control contrast. I1, I3 and I4 are met: 21 substance-dependent adults performed BART during fMRI, with group-level whole-brain longitudinal task maps. These within-group longitudinal comparisons are not contrasts against rest or fixation.

E6 met: reported whole-brain GLM results compare sleep-deprived and rested-wakefulness sessions, including the state-by-active/control risk-modulation interaction. No accompanying unmasked whole-brain task effect within either session is demonstrated. Risky BART fMRI, active-pump versus nonreward control-pump contrasts, and voxelwise group analyses meet I1, I2 and I3; the adult sample meets I4. Additional PPI, correlations and mediation do not supply the missing within-session task effect. The supplied tables directory is empty, but the complete Methods and Results explicitly describe the reported session comparisons.

I2 not met: the condition comparison contrasts otherwise identical BART pump decisions following negative versus positive feedback, not an admitted risky > safe, high-risk > low-risk, risk > certainty, or risk-task > active-control contrast. Pump number is a control parametric modulator, not a reported qualifying risk contrast. I1, I3, and I4 are met: adolescents performed the BART during fMRI, with group-level whole-brain task effects in Table 1. E1 is not met because a direct feedback-history condition comparison is reported, although it does not meet I2.

I2 not met and E1 met: BART pump and cash-out conditions are modeled separately against the implicit intertrial baseline; no admitted condition-versus-condition or active-control comparison is demonstrated. Table 2 reports group whole-brain main task effects (I3 met), so E4, E5 and E6 do not apply. Human fMRI during risky choice meets I1, and the child/adolescent sample qualifies under I4.

I2 not met: a qualifying condition-versus-condition or risk-task-versus-active-control contrast is not demonstrated. Although white-balloon control events were modeled, reported imaging findings concern pump-number parametric modulation and its association with network fractional anisotropy. These do not establish an admitted categorical contrast. Human BART fMRI, the adult sample, and whole-brain group analyses satisfy I1, I4, and I3; neither structural connectivity nor the presence of control trials alone supplies the missing contrast.

I2 not_met: Tables 3–7 report parametric trends in category distance, motion coherence and accuracy, or feature interactions. Figure 8 contrasts parametric modulation across salience contexts. No admitted direct hard > easy, low-coherence > high-coherence, or perceptual-task > active-control contrast is demonstrated. I1 and I4 met: adults performed dot-motion categorization during fMRI. I3 met: group voxelwise task activation maps and coordinate tables are reported, with maps masked by the positive main effect of task.

I2 not met: no admitted condition-versus-condition or decision-versus-active-control contrast was demonstrated. The reported whole-brain effects are parametric modulations by stimulus quality, accuracy and response time, with additional ROI/model correlations. A negative stimulus-quality slope is not a reported hard > easy condition contrast. Human participants performed perceptual choices during fMRI (I1 met), and group-level whole-brain results and eligible adults are documented (I3 and I4 met).
